questions.question: Summarise the facts about magnets and metals that the examination tests, including poles and fields, ferrous and non-ferrous metals, domains and how a magnet is made and destroyed.
questions.expected_answer: A magnet has a north and a south pole where its force is strongest; like poles repel and unlike poles attract, and a freely suspended magnet points north because the Earth is a magnet, which is how a compass works. The magnetic field is the region where the magnet exerts a force, drawn as lines from north to south closest where strongest, and cutting a magnet gives two magnets each with two poles. Only ferrous metals such as iron and steel, with nickel and cobalt, are attracted; copper, brass, aluminium, lead, zinc, gold and silver are non-ferrous and are not, which is the basis of magnetic sorting. Iron contains domains, tiny magnets that cancel when jumbled and add when aligned; stroking a nail in one direction aligns them to make a magnet, and hammering, heating or dropping scatters them. Soft iron magnetises and demagnetises easily and suits electromagnet cores; hard steel keeps its magnetism and suits permanent magnets.

questions.question: Describe the parts and symbols of a simple circuit, the difference between series and parallel, and how an electromagnet works, is strengthened and compares with a permanent magnet.
questions.expected_answer: A simple circuit has a cell as energy source, a conductor to carry current, a switch to control it and an output such as a bulb or buzzer, and current flows only when the loop is closed. Symbols: a cell as a long thin positive line and a short thick line, a switch as a gap with a slanted line drawn open, a bulb as a circle with a cross, a buzzer as a half circle, wires as ruled lines with right-angle corners. Series components share one current so extra bulbs dim; a parallel branch receives the full cell voltage. Metals conduct and plastic, rubber, glass and dry wood insulate. A current produces a magnetic field around a wire; coiling it into a solenoid concentrates the field into a switchable bar magnet whose poles swap when current reverses; a soft iron core aligns its domains and multiplies the field hundreds of times. It is strengthened by more turns, more current and a soft iron core, weakened by opposed turns, a non-ferrous core or shorted turns. Unlike a permanent magnet it can be switched off, adjusted and reversed, so the crane can release its load, but it needs a supply. Uses include bells, relays, scrap cranes, loudspeakers and motors.

questions.question: Define mechanical advantage and its trade, explain why a crank is a second-class lever and a pulley a wheel and axle, distinguish fixed and movable pulleys, and give the crane's chain of advantage.
questions.expected_answer: Mechanical advantage is load divided by effort, without unit; multiplying force by a factor makes the effort move further by the same factor, and advantages in a chain multiply. A second-class lever has the load between pivot and effort and always multiplies force. A crank is an arm at right angles to an axle with a handle at its end; its pivot is the axle, its load acts at the drum close to the axle and its effort at the handle far out, so it is a second-class lever bent into a circle with advantage equal to handle radius over drum radius. A pulley is a grooved wheel turning on an axle with a rope in the groove, a wheel and axle used to guide rope with little friction. A fixed pulley changes only direction, advantage one; a movable pulley hangs on the load and halves effort while doubling distance; the advantage of a system is the number of rope sections supporting the load, and friction makes the measured value slightly less. In the crane the crank gives about six and the fixed tip pulley one, a total of six, on a frame strengthened by tubes, triangulation, gussets and a weighted base.
